Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy . If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off) , respectively. LG B6E OLED TV Where to Buy: $1399.99 $699.99 at Best Buy (55-inch) $1899.99 $999.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $2699.99 $1499.99 at Best Buy (77-inch) Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6 , the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. items.originalTitle: All Hail Philomena Cunk, the Perfect Fake Newswoman for Our Age of Ignorance
items.author: Judy Berman
items.title: All Hail Philomena Cunk, the Perfect Fake Newswoman for Our Age of Ignorance
items.summary: Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix In the future, when some documentary series in whatever medium succeeds television looks back at the current decade in public discourse, it might name our era the Age of Ignorance. The crank shouting nonsense from atop a soapbox is, of course, nothing new. What’s unique to our time is how vast the audiences for these bloviators have become. We’ve got Alix Earle , with about 15 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, bragging about never having read a book. (Even if it wasn’t strictly true, how telling that she would let us believe it.) We’ve got Joe Rogan , by many measures the most popular podcaster out there—a guy who has platformed pandemic misinformation and had to apologize for using racial slurs — influencing nationwide elections . Just last week , Fox News star turned YouTuber Tucker Carlson entertained the possibility that the Smithsonian is suppressing evidence of the existence of Goliath-like giants. To which Philomena Cunk says: “Hold my snake oil.” The world-famous British TV presenter described by the Guardian as “ iconically stupid ” is back on Netflix and BBC Two with Cunk on Cinema , a six-part docuseries in which she gripes that reading subtitles makes it impossible to concentrate on one’s phone and pronounces D.W. Griffith’s KKK mash note The Birth of a Nation a “typically woke Hollywood fantasy.” (In what may or may not be a nod to viewers’ short attention spans, episodes top out at 15 minutes and can be binged in less time than it takes to watch most films.) Cunk is so incompetent, it’s hilarious. But unlike the personalities listed above, she’s meant to be funny—because she is a fictional character played by Diane Morgan. And although she was conceived when Earle was a tween and Carlson had bosses to answer to, she has since become the perfect fake newswoman to send up our Age of Ignorance. She may not be a real human being, but Cunk has had the kind of rise broadcast journalists dream about. After making her name in 2013 as an astonishingly dim yet opinionated commentator on Black Mirror creator Charlie Brooker ’s BBC Two comedy news show Weekly Wipe , she leveled up to hosting mockumentaries like Cunk on Shakespeare and Cunk on Britain , all helmed by Brooker. Like the other thought leaders we trust to guide us through complex topics on screen, in her solo efforts, Cunk combines her own explanations and analyses (“If the Tudors were the Kardashians of their time, this was their Kim: Henry of Eight”) with real expert interviews. “How important are the words in a Shakespeares [sic] play?” she once asked the venerable Shakespearean actor Simon Russell Beale. “Could you do it without the words?” In early 2023, she broke UK containment, arriving on Netflix with her own, let’s say, unique, series-length take on world history, Cunk on Earth . Two years later, her special Cunk on Life dared to ask big questions about nature and the universe—the implicit one being: What would Planet Earth be like if Sir David Attenborough had the intellect of a microorganism? Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix Philomena Cunk is a very British creation, in the tradition of Steve Coogan’s boorish TV-presenter character Alan Partridge and Sacha Baron Cohen ’s Da Ali G Show alter egos. From SNL ’s “Weekend Update” to The Daily Show , America’s news-satire tradition favors comedians telling dark jokes about current events in their own voices. But by the time she crossed the Atlantic, three years ago, U.S. audiences were primed to make Cunk a cult-comedy hero stateside, circulating her quotes and searching YouTube for morsels of her earlier work. Cunk on Life even scored a pair of Emmy nominations . It’s true that Baron Cohen broke out bigger in the U.S., during the 2000s, especially with his ingenuously inappropriate Kazakh reporter character, Borat. But his heyday coincided with a golden age of confrontational political satire, when Michael Moore broke box office records with documentaries built around interviews that embarrassed conservative icons like Charlton Heston and culture jammers like the Yes Men captured their elaborate anti-corporate hoaxes in feature films. Baron Cohen did something similar. As Baron Cohen wrote in an essay for TIME that coincided with the October release of his feature Ali G: Who Iz I? : “Each of my characters has a specific mechanism to encourage people to drop their guards and show what they really believe, prejudices and all.” In one notorious Ali G Show stunt, Borat got the patrons of an Arizona honky-tonk singing and clapping along to a song about throwing Jews down a well (though some later said they were behaving as directed or always knew it was all a bit). Morgan has a different agenda. She rarely humiliates the experts she interviews, who are generally in on the joke but, as in real news programs, aren’t given the questions in advance. Sure, she does occasionally mystify someone. In Cunk on Cinema , that person is Michael Bay , who at one point exclaims: “These are odd questions!” Most of the time, Cunk only embarrasses herself, though she’s too dim to realize it. The cringe comedy comes from the way the character makes the leading minds in every field behave as though the idiotic non sequiturs she imposes on them are worth engaging with. They’re too polite (or leery of coming off as elitists) not to. And when they do ever-so-gently push back, she tends to perform offendedness. “What was the Soviet Onion?” she asks a history professor in Cunk on Earth . She must mean the Soviet Union, he replies. “I don’t wanna be rude,” Cunk counters, despite much evidence to the contrary, “but I think you’re mansplaining a bit.” As Brooker has said : “The strange thing about Cunk is she’s sort of weirdly in charge of things, even if she’s speaking to a professor or whatever.” Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix Between interviews, she pontificates in the tones of a veteran newsreader, albeit one who has no understanding of the subject on which she’s been asked to extemporize. Cunk on Cinema will be extra entertaining to anyone who’s ever read a book or taken a survey course on the history of film, because of how deftly it plays on the field’s tropes and touchstones. Stanley Kubrick ca. 2001: A Space Odyssey is described offhandedly as a “groovy young director.” She refers to Soviet montage master Sergei Eisenstein’s landmark silent film Battleship Potemkin as Batsh-t Pumpkin , “one of cinema’s unwatchable masterpieces.” You needn’t have a Ph.D in Cinema Studies to appreciate the humor Brooker and Morgan wring out of Cunk’s hopelessness with names and titles. Wayne John, Marlo Brandon, E Dot T Dot (a.k.a. E.T. ). Quentin Tarantino , she informs us, “is Italian for five spiders.” If you’ve ever listened to a TikToker with no medical training evangelize unregulated peptide injections, you’ll see mirrored in Cunk the blithe confidence of a person who’s getting rich repackaging their ignorance as subversive truth-telling. When she wonders, “Was James Dean born a teenager?,” it’s a benign version of the level of question we typically get from podcast hosts who spend three-hour episodes credulously “hearing out” conspiracy theorists. Now, as you might expect from a writing team led by the Black Mirror guy, she’s got artificial intelligence to hallucinate along with her. In Cunk on Cinema , she insists to Die Hard screenwriter Steven E. de Souza that the all-American genius of silent comedy Buster Keaton spoke in a Cornish accent, then plays him the AI audio to “prove” it. I don’t want to minimize the brilliance of Morgan’s deadpan performance or Brooker’s jokes, which approach the linguistic density of poetry and tend to contain sneaky insights that would be lost on the character giving voice to them. ( Marilyn Monroe , says Cunk, “effortlessly blended sex appeal, vulnerability, comic timing, and innocence into one irresistible package for men to destroy.”) Yet I suspect so many of us love to laugh at Cunk because, for once in this choose-your-own-facts decade, the joke is on the fool or cynic with outsize influence instead of on anyone fed up with the latter contingent’s misinformation and glibness and idiocy and self-promotion at any cost. There’s a difference between thoughtful questions and thoughtless ones, informed opinions and hysterical polemic, challenging authority on principle and mindless contrarianism for personal gain. And it’s a relief to be reminded that someone still knows it.

Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

items.title: What Are the Masculine Virtues?
items.summary: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube One of the things that President Trump seems to admire most about his embattled defense secretary is Pete Hegseth’s vision of warrior masculinity, a vision Hegseth has attempted to impose on the military, through the firing of qualified high-ranking female officers, the denigration of long-established rules of engagement, and even the proposed screening of service members’ testosterone levels. These efforts are taking place at a time when many young American men are facing a very real crisis, but they don’t seem to have landed among their target audience: Male voters younger than 30 swung 40 percent toward Democrats in the midterms, one of the election’s largest such demographic shifts. In this episode of The Permanent Questions , David Brooks talks with Phil Klay, a Marine Corps veteran, National Book Award–winning novelist and story writer, and close observer of the effects that our 21st-century wars have had on American soldiers. Klay explains why Hegseth’s version of manhood is bad for men (and the military), why warfare can never be stripped of its moral meaning, and why love is the greatest masculine virtue. The following is a transcript of the episode: David Brooks: There are at least three important things going on in America right now. The first is that men are struggling. Lots of young men are out of the labor force entirely. Lots of young men are depressed. Suicide rates for young men are vastly higher than suicide rates for women. So that’s one thing going on. Second, we’re living with the consequences of probably three failed wars in the 21st century. There was the war in Iraq, the war in Afghanistan, and currently the war in Iran. That means there are a lot of young men—and women—who’ve been through those wars, who fought in those wars, who are trying to live with the consequences. This is a culture that is hurting in a lot of different ways. And along comes Donald Trump. Sometimes I think the Trump administration is a big advertisement for a certain sort of masculinity. It purports to be a solution to our cultural problems—that we’re gonna have a bunch of manly men and womanly women and we’ll return to a kind of gender relations that, according to some people, were healthier. Personally, I’m not particularly thrilled with what Pete Hegseth and Donald Trump are selling. I’d like a different social ideal, especially for guys. I’d like a different masculine ideal than the ones being offered today. To figure out how we could get to a healthier masculinity, I’m gonna hash it out with Phil Klay. Phil is a Marine veteran of Iraq. He served as a public affairs officer in the Anbar Province between 2007 and 2008 during the surge. When he returned home, he became a writer. His collection of short stories called Redeployment won the National Book Award in 2014. His most recent book of nonfiction essays is Uncertain Ground: Citizenship in an Age of Endless, Invisible War . He was recently selected to become the president of PEN America. It’s a real pleasure to welcome Phil Klay to this table. Phil Klay: Thank you for having me. Brooks: Manhood is in dispute. What should men be like? What should people be like? How do you be honorable? It seems to me there have been a series of social ideals that young men in particular were supposed to follow and this was held up as their social ideal. If you want to be a young man, be like this guy. You go back to ancient Greece, you got Achilles. He’s a rageful warrior. Then you got Pericles, who’s a magnanimous man. The magnanimous man serves his country. Magnanimous man is kind of aloof and standoffish. George Washington is our version of this. Then you go to Jesus and St. Francis. You get a very different masculine ideal, which is about compassion and peace. Jewish prophets and sages, which is like an intellectual ideal. You go to the Renaissance, you’ve got the courtier. There was this book—I’ve always wanted to write a book like this—Castiglione. Klay: I’ve read that. It’s quite something, Brooks: How to be a courtier, how to be elegant and graceful. Klay: Sprezzatura—you do everything effortlessly. Brooks: Right. Chivalric knights like Lancelot, and that’s an ideal. Then you get the 18th-century Enlightenment. You got a Ben Franklin kinda guy who studies everything on the Earth. He’s curious about things. Then you get my hero, the gentleman in Trollope, and Trollope novels always revolve around a gentleman who is not highborn necessarily, but who has a virtuous life. But my baby needs clothes.” So there’s that. And then the broader question is: You’re in war, you’re making decisions over life and death, you know people who died, and then it failed. So even though it felt like the most important thing, none of it mattered in terms of that higher purpose that you were supposed to be fighting for. That was the only reason to send you there. Brooks: I would say you had purpose and then sort of had it taken away. And I would say a lot of young guys never had a sense of purpose. If you know why you’re here, then you can handle whatever setbacks. But if you don’t know your “why,” then you really don’t know. Klay: It’s purposeless suffering that’s unendurable. Brooks: Fifty-eight percent of college students say they have no sense of meaning in their life. Klay: At a broader level, I think that there’s a kind of general question, but America has always been a project toward the future, toward a more perfect union. There’s this sort of question of what America is in terms of the sum total of its parts is not what America is. What America is is that collective effort toward something. And I feel like that is an undernourished idea in American political life. This idea of these founding ideals, abstractions, feels less present for us. What kind of nation are we trying to achieve at the broadest level? And then there’s the questions of individual purpose within our lives and in modern America. Brooks: It’s famously said that what is true of America, that we’re incredibly cheerful and optimistic and upbeat—and that is no longer true, maybe because of the defeats we’ve suffered. But I think that sense of pessimism and alienation, which is quite widespread— Klay: I’ll say another thing about education. There is a kind of relentless utilitarian pressure on education, which of course makes sense because it’s a tough world out there. You gotta get a job, you gotta make a living, right? If you go to college, you gotta pay for it. College is unbelievably expensive these days. But for a young person, it’s like: All right, there’s this somewhat meritocratic system that you’re gonna put an unbelievable amount of effort into, right? And the education that we’re giving you bleaches out the sort of humanistic disciplines day by day which are the ones that are all about what life is actually for, that are trying to attune you to notions of meaning, purpose, and beauty. That kind of division is only more intense. Education has become more utilitarian, has had more of that pressure put on it. And yet, it is the human, humanistic disciplines that are ultimately so important for giving us a reason to wanna do any of that stuff. Brooks: I think that’s why I admire the Marines or soldiers, sailors, whatever. For a young person today, I think they need—we all need this at no matter what age—the kind of moral seriousness that you mentioned, that if you’re in the Marines or whatever service and somebody’s getting killed, you have to know: Will this person risk their life for me? That is the core of integrity, and that’s the core of courage, and that’s the core of honor. If you don’t put that in front of young people, and I think especially young guys, that the society may be screwed up in a million ways, but today you can behave honorably or not honorably, courageously or not courageously, compassionately or not compassionately. And so everything is a moral test. It seems to me a lot of the alienation we see among young men is not knowing what virtue should I shoot for, what’s relevant in my life. I have this argument all the time with people. What’s the key virtue? We all have our own recipe of virtues. I know a lot of people who say courage. If you don’t have the courage to overcome risks, you’re not going to take chances in life. You’re probably not going to ask somebody out on a date. Courage is really important. My own personal favorite is humility. I think that’s the core virtue around which all others are based. To me, humility is not thinking lowly of yourself. It’s having radical self-awareness from a position of other centeredness. It’s the ability to step outside yourself and say, “Well, I’m actually kind of strong in this realm, but I’m actually kind of weak in that realm.” So you know yourself accurately, and you know what you need to work on, you know what you can do, and how should you devote your life. Abraham Lincoln was a humble man, but he also knew he was kinda special in some ways. I don’t know how you would think about the virtues in your life or the virtues you saw around you or the virtues you see celebrated in civilian society, which you are now a member of. Klay: Love. Brooks: Oh, interesting. Why do you say that? Klay: I think that’s what everything decent flows from. Brooks: Now I realize I have to update my answer. Klay: And by the way, I mentioned Elliot Ackerman earlier. He was talking to me about courage, which you mentioned as a primary virtue. Elliot’s got a Silver Star and a Bronze Star, and he’s done outrageous things. And he was talking about in the Second Battle of Fallujah a Marine has to cross this highway, right? And it’s very dangerous ’cause it’s open, there’s a lot of places, and he gets shot. And another Marine goes out to pull him, and that Marine gets shot too. So now it’s pretty obvious what’s gonna happen if you try and rescue those guys. There’s this enemy sniper waiting for you. And another Marine goes out and pulls those guys back. Elliot was saying like, “Why do people do that?” Because there’s fear on the one hand. And then, because on the other hand, there’s courage. And he says, “I’ve never felt the emotion courage. That’s not a thing. I’m never feeling brave today.” He says, “Why did somebody do that?” Because they love each other, right? When you are in this tight-knit unit that’s trained together and been through these things, you develop this intense bond and love for one another. And that for him was the opposite of fear. Brooks: It’s so interesting you say that. Again, my head is full of studies. It’s not a good way to live. But there was a famous study called the Grant Study, which was done at Harvard, and they took young men—in those days, Harvard was all male—and they followed them through their lives. Among those Harvard underclassmen were people like John F. Kennedy, Ben Bradlee, who edited the Washington Post. Because they graduated into the war, a lot of them entered the Army, and they wanted to figure out what traits correlate to promotion in the military. They think, “Well, is it IQ?” Nope. “Physical strength?” Nope. “Is it courage to the extent that they can measure this?” Nope. The number one factor that correlates with promotion in the military in World War II for these men was love of mother, warmth of family home. Klay: That’s amazing. Brooks: And basically, the guys who had learned love from mom knew how to extend love to their men. And when you talked about the utilitarianism of our educational system, it seems to me we’ve downplayed that school should be about helping students find things to fall in love with. That by itself would, especially people who are adrift, give them direction—’cause, you know: Yeah, this is what I love . I don’t know. Is it too probing or intimate to ask you if you had to come up with your own list of the things? Klay: Things that I love? Family. My wife and kids and broader family. My friends, my country, books, novels, a good sentence. I’m coaching two soccer teams right now—two Little League soccer teams. And I’m loving that. Yeah. With my mother-in-law as my assistant coach. Brooks: Oh really? Wow. I think over the last 26 years, we’ve been in this century, or maybe since 9/11, when the 21st century really started—we have taken some blows as a country. And we’ve become more alienated and disillusioned. But I do think these eternal verities apply, and that human nature hasn’t changed. And the seeking of these kind of moral virtues, but just plain old love, falling in love with things, that would go a long way to making young men and young women live in a better society. I don’t know if you’re hopeful. Klay: I’m sort of short-term pessimistic, long-term optimistic, you know? I say that. I’ve been writing about warfare for my entire career, and nobody’s taken my advice yet. Maybe my kids will figure it out. They’re pretty smart. Brooks: Phil Klay, thank you for being at our table at The Permanent Questions . Klay: Thank you so much. Brooks: There was a moment in the middle of this conversation that I will not soon forget. I was talking to Phil about what he felt when he thought about how the lives of him and the men and women he fought with in Iraq were treated, and the word that came out of his mouth was rage . And if you’re listening to this without visuals, you may have heard long silences, and that was Phil trying to collect his emotions. It’s been a long time since he’s been in Iraq, and very clearly, those emotions were still on the surface and very raw. Phil once wrote that when you enlist in the military, it’s an act of faith toward your country, an act of faith that your country will guard your life and protect you and treat you as the precious thing you are. I think for Phil and for a lot of people—the veterans of that war, Afghanistan, maybe some of the others—that act of faith has been broken by a country that was not careful in protecting and caring for the men and women who enlisted in these battles. And you can see the rage at this betrayal still close to the surface in his mind, and I think in a lot of people’s minds. And I was also struck by when I asked what his core virtue is, and he did not respond with bitterness, he did not respond with alienation, he just said “love.” I take that to be a very hard-headed rejoinder to what happens when you begin to lose faith. You find things to love, and you remind yourself why, despite it all, you love your country. I found it very moving, that mixture of rage and love. So thanks so much for joining us for this week’s conversation with Phil Klay. The Permanent Questions is produced and edited by The Atlantic in partnership with Yale University. items.author: Keza MacDonald
items.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
items.summary: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.

Cousins revealed that when he signed with the Atlanta Falcons in 2024, he sold his house through a neighbor without ever putting it on the open market. The 38-year-old said his neighbor told him he had someone who could buy his house immediately, so Cousins sold it without ever listing it. Margit Brandt, a luxury real estate agent, said that Cousins may have gotten a little lucky finding an off the market buyer for his house so quickly, but there are many advantages to selling a home off-market. There's photos on Zillow and online of like what your living room and your kitchen and your closet, like all these personal spaces," Brandt told OutKick in a recent interview. "So for someone like Kirk Cousins to have someone come in off market and not have to like open his dress, so to speak, right, in terms of his home on the market, his name being out there. I think that's appealing." Brandt is based in Palm Beach, Florida, and said her team has sold $1 billion worth of homes this year, with about a third of those sales completed off-market. When looking to sell a home, Brandt said she taps into her relationships if a client initially requests an off-market sale. THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! "We have like a private portfolio for off-market properties. It's a safety thing." Cousins said at the end of his re-introductory press conference with the Minnesota Vikings that his wife, Julie, and their sons are staying in a hotel while she looks for a new home. items.author: Ebony Riddell Bamber
items.title: Oxford is platforming race baiter Nathan Cofnas. I know how corrosive that will be for Black students | Ebony Riddell Bamber
items.summary: In the 90s, I studied under the notorious racist lecturer Frank Ellis. At a time when I should have felt liberated to explore, it chipped away at my self-esteem In 2006, Dr Frank Ellis, who taught Russian and Slavonic studies at the University of Leeds, was suspended from his post as lecturer after he told a student newspaper that he supported the theory that Black people were less intelligent than white people. In the pages of the Guardian at the time, he was described as a “lecturer who insisted that black people and women were genetically inferior”. This was six years after his views first received national coverage . When I saw Ellis’s views make it to the national press, I felt angry. I had known Ellis was a racist because when I was a student of Russian studies between 1996 and 2000, he taught many of my classes and I had to endure hearing his views on a regular basis. He would regularly tell us that nothing good had ever come out of Africa, and he would share how he wrote for white supremacist publications and attended conferences in the US alongside members of the Ku Klux Klan. items.originalTitle: Entangled Past: how descendants of enslaved and enslavers in Grenada embarked on journey of repair

items.title: Entangled Past: how descendants of enslaved and enslavers in Grenada embarked on journey of repair
items.summary: In their book, the historian Nicole Phillip and journalist Laura Trevelyan use connected experiences to show how reparations can work in practice When the Grenadian historian Nicole Phillip opened an email from the then BBC journalist Laura Trevelyan in 2022, she uncovered a connection that stretched back centuries. Their ancestors had stood on opposite sides of enslavement in Grenada: Phillip’s among Africans forcibly taken from their homes and enslaved, Trevelyan’s among the British families who profited from a system that inflicted unspeakable cruelty and inhumanity on generations of enslaved Africans.
